## RFC 1958, judged by the hard-to-vary method

**1. The question, frozen.** The title and opening make central: *What are the architectural principles of the Internet?* Range: the public Internet, ARPANET (1971) to June 1996. What is asked: which guidelines hold and should guide new protocol design. The document answers more than one question — §2 asks "is there an architecture at all?" and §1 adds a meta-claim — but I take the principle-list as central. This is a design rationale (by-domain §2) with a few explanations embedded, not one causal story.

**2. The explanation in parts.** In the author's words: "the goal is connectivity, the tool is the Internet Protocol, and the intelligence is end to end." Parts: (a) the end-to-end argument; (b) fate-sharing — no network state that outlives a temporary outage; (c) datagrams over virtual circuits; (d) one and only one Internet-level protocol; (e) layering independent of hardware; (f) a catalogue of ~35 numbered prescriptions (§3–6); (g) the §1 meta-claims (constant change; evolution caused the success; connectivity is its own reward). Jobs named: connectivity, interoperability, scale, survival of partial failure, end-to-end security.

**3. Part by part.** One mark each.

| Part | Mark — and why |
|---|---|
| End-to-end argument (2.3) | **Borrowed** — rests on [Saltzer], cited, not tested here |
| Fate-sharing (2.3) | **Held** — removing it breaks "applications survive partial network failures" |
| Datagrams over virtual circuits (2.3) | **Held if** — only because fate-sharing holds, and that job is asserted, not tested |
| One Internet-level protocol (2.2) | **Held if** — by "uniform, seamless multi-vendor operation," a job the author asserts |
| Layering independent of hardware (2.2) | **Held** — by "interconnect any new transmission medium" |
| Circular dependencies (3.11) | **Held** — by the DNS-depends-on-routing case |
| End-to-end security (6.2) | **Held if** — by "endpoints, not carriers, must be trusted" |
| Constant change (§1) | **Loose** — a frozen snapshot does the same job; it covers either outcome |
| "Evolution caused the success" (§1, 2.1) | **Loose** — fitted to the one case that happened; no change named against it |
| "Connectivity is its own reward" (2.1) | **Loose** — read backwards from observed growth |
| Prescriptions 3.1–3.10, 3.12, 3.14, 4.1–4.5, 5.1–5.4, 6.1, 6.3–6.5 | **Fixed** — set by the author, no job or test given; a job could be supplied later |
| Conventions: ASCII names (4.3), shared notation (3.13), unpatented tech (5.1) | **Loose** — free and harmless |
| "Running code before standard" (3.14) | **Held if** — by "spec must interoperate"; the memo's own Informational status is the exception |

I removed the catalogue in groups; each item goes without losing a named job — that is why they are *fixed*, not idle. No part took **idle**, **two routes** or **unknown**.

**4. Whole-explanation checks.**
- **Flip.** Would the document read the same if the Internet had lost to a centrally planned rival? "Constant change" and "evolution caused success" cover either outcome, so those two explain nothing alone. The end-to-end core does not flip easily: it commits to what happens under network failure.
- **Direction.** 2.1 argues from observed growth to the value "connectivity is its own reward." That answers *what can we tell*, not *what produces it*. Fine for one, not the other.
- **Answer in the starting points.** 2.2 wants one protocol "for uniform seamless operations"; the conclusion (one protocol) sits under the premise (uniformity) under another name.
- **Where jobs came from.** Connectivity and scale are given/fixed; the document adds no job of its own and never turns the tests on itself.
- **Pairs that pull.** 3.5 (simplest) against 3.3 (scale to millions) and 3.12 (self-describing). 3.2 (choose one way) against 3.1 (heterogeneity) and against 2.2's own allowance for a "fundamentally new" protocol. 3.7 (almost-complete now) against finding a perfect solution. The document names none of these joints or says which gives way.
- **Catch-alls.** 3.2's "unless there is a good technical reason not to," and 3.5's "when in doubt," absorb any case and carry no gauge. No reading is named that would show them swallowing a job.
- **Change list.** It leaves out the one thing a list of principles most needs: which principle wins when two conflict. That omission is declared ("various guidelines," a snapshot), so it is an honest limit, not a silent narrowing.
- **Rivals.** §2.1 names "no architecture, only a tradition," but nothing on the list tells the two apart; at this level they are one explanation. The author says so.
- **Where from.** The end-to-end core is built and borrowed ([Saltzer], [Clark]); "evolution caused success" is fitted to the single case; the numbered list is asserted.

**5. What would make it harder to vary.** Give each load-bearing claim one poke — a change that should matter and one that should not. For end-to-end: cut a link in the middle of the network — do the endpoints still recover (should), and does a better middlebox make recovery unnecessary (should not, if the claim holds). Give 3.2 and 3.5 a gauge: name the reading at which "a good technical reason" or "in doubt" is saving the rule. For 3.5 against 3.3, say which gives way.

**6. What this does not show.** Hard to vary is not true. Several prescriptions here may be right and still unheld; the held core may be wrong.

**7. One next step.** Ask the editor to mark each numbered principle **held** (with the job named), **loose**, or **fixed** — starting with 3.5 and 3.2, whose "unless…" clauses are the catch-alls.
